# SK2153 — An IQueryable is silently degraded to IEnumerable

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A deferred LINQ operator binds to Enumerable on a receiver whose static type is IQueryable, so the rest of the query stops translating and runs in the client.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `PossibleUnintendedQueryableAsEnumerable` (`resharper_possible_unintended_queryable_as_enumerable_highlighting`) |

## Why

Once one operator binds to `System.Linq.Enumerable`, the provider has already been asked to enumerate everything it has: the `Where` that was meant to become a `WHERE` clause becomes a full table read, and every operator after it runs on the wire's output. Nothing fails, nothing warns, and the only symptom is a query that got slower in proportion to the table. It is the most expensive silent mistake in data-access code, and it is normally introduced by passing a `Func<T, bool>` where an `Expression<Func<T, bool>>` was needed — a change of one word at a declaration far from the call.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
Func<Order, bool> open = o => o.Status == 0;
return context.Orders.Where(open).Take(20);
```

Write:

```csharp
Expression<Func<Order, bool>> open = o => o.Status == 0;
return context.Orders.Where(open).Take(20);
```

## The ReSharper mapping

⚠ The export sets `resharper_possible_unintended_queryable_as_enumerable_highlighting = suggestion` and this rule defaults to `warning`. ReSharper reports the whole family of implicit `IQueryable` → `IEnumerable` conversions, including the deliberate ones, so a low severity is how that inspection stays usable; this rule reports only a *composable* operator that bound to `Enumerable`, which is never deliberate, so it can afford the severity the consequence deserves. docs/plan/16 § Q5.

## When it does not fire

⚠ **`AsEnumerable` is excluded by name, and the claim that it was excluded "structurally" was wrong.** What the receiver's type excludes is everything chained *after* an `.AsEnumerable()` — that result is an `IEnumerable<T>`, so no operator downstream of it can reach this rule. The call **itself** is an `Enumerable` extension returning `IEnumerable<T>` on an `IQueryable` receiver, which is the rule's exact shape: the first version reported `.AsEnumerable()`, the one call that is the sanctioned way to say "client-side, deliberately". A rule that reports its own escape hatch is a rule that reports its own fix, and the negative fixture is what caught it. `ToList()` and `ToArray()` need no such exclusion, because their return types are not sequences. ⚠ **Only operators that return a sequence are reported.** `ToList`, `ToArray`, `ToDictionary`, `ToHashSet` have no `Queryable` counterpart and binding them to `Enumerable` is the intended way to materialise — reporting those would report every correct query in the repository. The finding needs the invoked method's return type to be `IEnumerable<T>` or `IOrderedEnumerable<T>`, which is exactly the set of operators whose result *could* still have been a query. ⚠ **Scalar operators are silent even though `Queryable` has them.** `Count()`, `Any()`, `First()` bound to `Enumerable` on an `IQueryable` really do fetch the table, but they also appear at the end of chains this rule has already reported, and reporting both turns one defect into two findings. The composable operator is the one that begins the degradation. ⚠ **`hasFix: false`**: the repair is to change a delegate's declared type to `Expression<...>` at another declaration, or to accept the materialisation by writing `.AsEnumerable()` — a decision about intent that no edit can make. Inserting `.AsEnumerable()` would silence the rule while keeping the defect, which is the fix `skala fix` must never have.
